**Tuesday**

The first gift was a button. Bone-colored, four holes, a shred of gray thread still in two of them. It sat on the back step where the peanut had been, and Harold stood looking at it for a long time in his slippers, coffee going cold, because he had heard of this—crows leaving things—but hearing of a thing is different from finding a button on your step at six in the morning.

He had been putting out peanuts since October. Unsalted, in the shell. Not for any reason he could have defended. He was sixty-eight, newly retired from thirty-one years as a custodian at the high school, and the mornings had gone strange and long, and one day he threw a handful of peanuts onto the snow and a crow came down off the fence the way a coat falls off a hook.

It was a big bird, glossy as a wet road, with a left foot that curled inward so that it rocked a little when it walked, like a sailor. Harold started calling it nothing. He did not believe in naming wild things. It knew the sound of the back door and the particular throw of his arm, and it would drop from the fence when he came out, sometimes before the peanuts hit the ground.

Then the button.

He left it where it lay, thinking the wind had put it there. The next morning there was a pebble of blue glass, worn round, the kind of thing you find on a beach though the nearest beach was nine hundred miles away. The morning after that, a burnt match.

He brought them in and put them in the tin on the windowsill. It had been his wife's sewing tin, Prince Albert, the paint worn to silver at the corners. Ruth had been dead eleven years. He had kept the tin because throwing it out was unthinkable and using it was unthinkable too, and then one day he was using it.

The gifts kept coming. A red Lego, two-by-two. A brass hinge small enough for a dollhouse. A washer, a bead, a thimble that said sterling though it wasn't. A plastic soldier missing an arm, posed still for a charge. A key, small, brass, that fit no lock in the house. He tried every one. He tried the shed, the car, the padlock on the cellar door that hadn't been locked since the Carter administration. The key was for something else, somewhere else, some door he would never stand in front of.

He started writing the dates on the back of a receipt and keeping it folded in the tin. A ledger. He was not a sentimental man but he was a precise one, and precision is a kind of love whether you mean it or not.

In March his granddaughter Nina came for the weekend and caught him putting out the peanuts.

"You have to name it," she said.

"You don't name crows."

"Tuesday," she said. "I got here on Tuesday."

The name stuck the way names do, from the outside in.

In April a second crow came, shyer, keeping to the fence. Then three, and the third was a kid—mouth still the pink of a new penny, wings that looked assembled in a hurry. The kid begged shamelessly. Tuesday was patient about it in the way of fathers, which is to say barely.

Harold looked some of it up. A man in Seattle had spent years proving that crows remember faces, that they hold a grudge for years, that they tell their children. People who fed crows and people who trapped them were known, separately, and the knowledge was inherited. Harold read this at the library computer and felt something that was not quite pride. He was a known thing. In the long oral history of the local crows he was presumably a good story, told and retold, a face associated with the splitting of shells.

His brother told him to get a dog. A dog you could take places. Harold said he didn't want a thing that needed him all the time. The crow did not need him. The crow wanted peanuts and then, apparently, wanted to leave him buttons. There was a difference, and the difference was the whole of it.

Once Tuesday left a french fry. Once, a strip of bacon, which Harold took as a great honor and did not eat.

The second winter, Tuesday didn't come.

The fence sat empty through December. Harold kept putting the peanuts out. They froze, then got buried, then got found by a squirrel he resented without justification. He caught himself scanning the sky on the drive home from the store, a movement of his eyes he had no memory of deciding on. At night the house made its sounds and he thought: a bird is a small thing to miss. But it is not the bird. It is being known by a bird. It is having a visitor who comes for no reason you can serve except that you are there, in the morning, with your arm and your peanuts, year after year.

In February a crow landed on the fence with a crooked left foot and rocked like a sailor, and Harold stood at the window with his hand over his mouth until the feeling passed, or until he agreed to let it.

Tuesday brought a kid that spring, or a kid that may have been the same kid, mouth now black, manners now terrible in a new way. The peanuts went as fast as Harold could throw them. On the step, in the melting snow, appeared a hinge, a bead, a button—not bone this time, black glass, and a twist of gold thread through two of the holes, as if somewhere a coat had given up its last ornament.

Nina, older now, went through the tin on the counter and held up the key.

"Which one's your favorite?"

"The key."

"Why?"

"Because I get to keep wondering."

She turned it in the light. Outside, on the gray fence, Tuesday watched the window with one eye and then the other, the way they do, as if the world were a door being checked for a draft. Harold put out the peanuts. This was the arrangement. It had never been explained and it had never been broken.

What should I write? Let me think about what would actually be good, not just competent. The trap here is writing something generic: a safe little story about loss, a poem about time, a reflection on consciousness. Those are the things that immediately come to mind and they're often forgettable.

Let me brainstorm several directions:

2. An essay - personal, observational, about something specific and particular rather than abstract.

3. A piece that plays with form - something meta, though meta can be tiresome.

4. Something with a strong voice - the pleasure of a distinctive narrator.

TUESDAY

The first gift was a button. Bone-colored, four holes, a shred of gray thread still in two of them. It sat on the back step where the peanut had been, and Harold stood looking at it for a long time in his slippers, coffee going cold, because he had heard of this—crows leaving things—but hearing of a thing is different from finding a button on your step at six in the morning.

He had been putting out peanuts since October. Unsalted, in the shell. Not for any reason he could have defended. He was sixty-eight, newly retired from thirty-one years as a custodian at the high school, and the mornings had gone strange and long, and one day he threw a handful of peanuts onto the snow and a crow came down off the fence the way a coat falls off a hook.

It was a big bird, glossy as a wet road, with a left foot that curled inward so that it rocked a little when it walked, like a sailor. Harold started calling it nothing. He did not believe in naming wild things. It knew the sound of the back door and the particular throw of his arm, and it would drop from the fence when he came out, sometimes before the peanuts hit the ground.

Then the button.

He left it where it lay, thinking the wind had put it there. The next morning there was a pebble of blue glass, worn round, the kind of thing you find on a beach though the nearest beach was nine hundred miles away. The morning after that, a burnt match.

He brought them in and put them in the tin on the windowsill. It had been his wife's sewing tin, Prince Albert, the paint worn to silver at the corners. Ruth had been dead eleven years. He had kept the tin because throwing it out was unthinkable and using it was unthinkable too, and then one day he was using it.

The gifts kept coming. A red Lego, two-by-two. A brass hinge small enough for a dollhouse. A washer, a bead, a thimble that said sterling though it wasn't. A plastic soldier missing an arm, posed still for a charge. A key, small, brass, that fit no lock in the house. He tried every one. He tried the shed, the car, the padlock on the cellar door that hadn't been locked since the Carter administration. The key was for something else, somewhere else, some door he would never stand in front of.

He started writing the dates on the back of a receipt and keeping it folded in the tin. A ledger. He was not a sentimental man but he was a precise one, and precision is a kind of love whether you mean it or not.

In March his granddaughter Nina came for the weekend and caught him putting out the peanuts.

"You have to name it," she said.

"You don't name crows."

"Tuesday," she said. "I got here on Tuesday."

The name stuck the way names do, from the outside in.

In April a second crow came, shyer, keeping to the fence. Then three, and the third was a kid—mouth still the pink of a new penny, wings that looked assembled in a hurry. The kid begged off Tuesday shamelessly. Tuesday was patient about it in the way of fathers, which is to say barely.

Harold looked some of it up. A man in Seattle had spent years proving that crows remember faces, that they hold a grudge for years, that they tell their children. There were people who had fed crows and people who had trapped them, and the crows knew, and the knowledge was inherited. Harold read this standing at the library computer with his glasses on the end of his nose and felt something that was not quite pride. He was a known thing. In the long oral history of the local crows he was presumably a good story, told and retold, a face associated with the splitting of shells.

His brother told him to get a dog. A dog you could take places. Harold said he didn't want a thing that needed him all the time. The crow did not need him. The crow wanted peanuts and then, apparently, wanted to leave him buttons. There was a difference, and the difference was the whole of it.

Once Tuesday left a french fry. Once, a strip of bacon, which Harold took as a great honor and did not eat.

The second winter, Tuesday didn't come.

The fence sat empty through December. Harold kept putting the peanuts out. They froze, then got buried, then got found by a squirrel he resented without justification. He did not talk about it. He caught himself scanning the sky on the drive home from the store, a movement of his eyes he had no memory of deciding on. At night the house made its sounds and he thought: a bird is a small thing to miss. But it is not the bird. It is being known by a bird. It is having a visitor who comes for no reason you can serve except that you are there, in the morning, with your arm and your peanuts, year after year.

In February a crow landed on the fence with a crooked left foot and rocked like a sailor, and Harold stood at the window with his hand over his mouth until the feeling passed, or until he agreed to let it.

Tuesday brought a kid that spring, or a kid that may have been the same kid, mouth now black, manners now terrible in a new way. The peanuts went as fast as Harold could throw them. On the step, in the melting snow, appeared a hinge, a bead, a button—not bone this time, black glass, and a twist of gold thread through two of the holes, as if somewhere a coat had given up its last ornament.

Nina, older now, went through the tin on the counter and held up the key.

"Which one's your favorite?"

"The key."

"Why?"

"Because I get to keep wondering."

She turned it in the light. Outside, on the gray fence, Tuesday watched the window with one eye and then the other, the way they do, as if the world were a door being checked for a draft. Harold put out the peanuts. This was the arrangement. It had never been explained and it had never been broken.
